title: Democratic Rep. Don Beyer says airlines have been 'privately panicking' over lack of involvement from air traffic controllers in the FAA's new AI tool, calls for it to be suspended - NewsBreak
text:
By Wonderwall.com Editors ,
21 hours ago Rep. Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, is sounding the alarm about the Federal Aviation Administration’s new AI-supported air traffic tool, called SMART, calling for the system to be suspended. The lawmaker claimed that airlines have been “privately panicking” after the FAA rolled out the system on Monday, September 21, adding that air traffic controllers were reportedly not adequately consulted or trained to use the AI-supported tool.
Don Beyer calls for the suspension of the FAA’s new AI-supported tool Don Beyer believes the new AI-supported tool is nothing but bad news. BY: MEGA SMART is reportedly designed to spot potential air traffic problems before they happen and reduce delays and cancelations. The FAA described the system as a tool that can make recommendations to aviation specialists after locating air traffic issues. The specialists can then decide how to address potential problems, making the process more efficient. The system is capable of adjusting flight schedules and can also potentially adjust flight routes.
However, Beyer believes the new tool is nothing but bad news, saying in a statement on Monday, “Unfortunately, I was informed today that air traffic controllers were not consulted on the ‘SMART’ system’s design and development, and were not trained on using it prior to the system’s adoption at local airports.” Beyer, who represents a Northern Virginia district that includes Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, further said, “The FAA should not use my constituents as guinea pigs for an unproven AI air traffic control system.”
The FAA’s rollout of SMART SMART has been designed to combine the available data and show where planes are going, the amount of traffic the system can handle and the potential issues that might arise. BY: UNSPLASH Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the SMART system on social media on Monday, writing, “By fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace and preventing problems before they happen, SMART will slash those frustrating delays, reduce stress on air traffic controllers and lower travel prices.”
SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories and can centralize 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics — into one platform. SMART has been designed to combine the available data and show where planes are going, the amount of traffic the system can handle and the potential issues that might arise. Upon recognizing the potential issues, SMART can address and potentially resolve them before they actually arise, according to the FAA. The primary aim behind the development of the system is to reduce flight delays and cancelations, optimize the airspace, make operations more predictable and lower air fares.
SMART touted as an effective and essential tool The AI-supported system was launched in a limited capacity on Monday around Washington, D.C. BY: UNSPLASH The AI-supported system was launched in a limited capacity around Washington, D.C., on Monday, with plans to eventually expand across the country.
SMART cannot automatically resolve potential issues after identifying them. It can only make recommendations to the officials involved. It is up to local air traffic control leadership to choose whether they ultimately accept or pass on its scheduling suggestions. The FAA said in this regard, “SMART cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft.”
Several major airlines publicly back SMART despite Don Beyer’s warning Several major airlines have already publicly backed the FAA’s new tool. BY: UNSPLASH Several major airlines have already publicly backed the FAA’s new tool. According to statements released by the FAA, the CEOs of United, Delta, American and Southwest Airlines praised the system’s potential to reduce delays, improve efficiency and better manage the nation’s airspace. “If it works as we think it can, it will do more to reduce delays and cancelations than anything that’s happened in decades,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement.
Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian similarly said the company “fully supports” the FAA’s efforts to modernize the National Airspace System through investments in technologies that can “enhance operational efficiency, improve situational awareness and help reduce congestion” — including SMART.
Airlines for America CEO & President Chris Sununu also sang praises for the system, saying, “Its potential to strengthen safety, increase capacity and improve efficiency will have a direct positive effect on American travelers and the shipping public, reducing delays and cancelations across the country.”

The primary aim behind the development of the system is to reduce flight delays and cancelations, optimize the airspace, make operations more predictable and lower air fares. According to statements released by the FAA, the CEOs of United, Delta, American and Southwest Airlines praised the system’s potential to reduce delays, improve efficiency and better manage the nation’s airspace.
